overview: Switzerland grew from a confederation of cantons into a modern federal state through war, negotiation and constitutional change. The old alliance was not yet the Switzerland established in 1848. These two map labels share a connected history, with the French-backed Helvetic Republic and later settlements clearly separated.

periods.title: The Old Confederation
periods.summary: Cantons and their subject territories belonged to a confederation rather than one centralized nation-state.

periods.title: Revolution and Mediation
periods.summary: French intervention replaced the old order with the Helvetic Republic in 1798; the 1803 settlement restored a federal arrangement.

periods.title: A renewed confederation
periods.summary: The Federal Treaty of 1815 preceded the Sonderbund War of 1847 and the new federal constitution.

periods.title: The federal state
periods.summary: The 1848 constitution established the modern federal state, whose political rights continued to change.

sections.title: Work, learning and the old cantons

items.text: A family’s home could also be a textile workshop. Merchants supplied raw material, sometimes lent looms, and paid for finished cloth according to quantity and quality. Children joined adults in production; working at home did not automatically mean choosing your own hours.

In eighteenth-century Appenzell, some weaving took place in low, humid cellars with narrow windows. Damp air helped the threads, even if it was hardly a luxury office. Embroidery required a different workspace with better light: the craft shaped the house.

Basel’s university was disrupted by the Reformation in 1529 and reopened under municipal oversight in 1532. Teaching did not simply disappear in between: Oswald Bär performed a public anatomical dissection in 1531. Religious and political upheaval could alter the classroom itself.

Education had costs that not every family could meet. Basel created scholarships for poor boys in 1533 using former ecclesiastical resources, and an Erasmus foundation supported needy students from 1538. These targeted arrangements were not universal access to university.

Erasmus’s New Testament appeared from Johann Froben’s Basel press in 1516 with Greek text and a new Latin version. Comparing manuscripts, editing type and organizing printing made this a collaborative scholarly achievement, not a book created by a lone author overnight.

The Greek manuscripts behind Basel scholarship had traveled. Material associated with John of Ragusa linked the city’s libraries to Byzantium. A printed page could therefore carry the results of journeys, copying and argument across several generations.

In 1799, during the Helvetic Republic, education minister Philipp Albert Stapfer sent schools a questionnaire of roughly sixty questions. More than 2,400 replies survive, mostly from teachers, describing lessons, personnel, local conditions and money. They preserve differences between real classrooms rather than one imaginary “Swiss school.”

The federal Factory Act of 1877 prohibited factory employment below age fourteen and limited the working day. Its scope matters: protection for factory children did not instantly abolish children’s work in farms or home industries. A law was an important change, not a magic off-switch.

A historical account of the Gubel institution at Neuägeri describes girls working and studying around demanding textile shifts. Reports of tired pupils make the conflict between production and learning visible. This is a specific institution, not evidence that every Swiss child lived the same way.

Industrial schedules helped create a market for foods that were quick to prepare. The museum’s account follows firms such as Maggi and includes a 1910 image of food production. Soup could become a factory product long before the microwave appeared.

Chocolate makers refined texture as well as flavor. Daniel Peter developed milk chocolate in the 1870s, while Rodolphe Lindt’s conching process of 1879 helped make it smoother. These were particular technical improvements, not proof that Switzerland invented every kind of chocolate.

A surviving nineteenth-century bidet at Jegenstorf Castle looks like mahogany furniture, with a removable ceramic basin and a cover. It belonged in a world of bedroom washing equipment. Fancy woodwork could conceal a very practical job; one castle object does not describe every household’s bathroom.

Swiss women gained the federal vote in 1971. Cantonal voting rights followed different paths: the Federal Court required Appenzell Innerrhoden to admit women in 1990, and women first participated in its cantonal assembly in 1991. “When women could vote” therefore needs a level of government.

German, constitution of 1848, article 4: “Alle Schweizer sind vor dem Gesetze gleich.” Translation: “All Swiss are equal before the law.” Parliament’s historical discussion reproduces the sentence and explains its limits: women were still excluded from political equality. A promise on paper and its reach in practice are different questions.

Latin, the title used for Erasmus’s 1516 edition: “Novum Instrumentum.” In this biblical context it means “New Testament.” The short title illustrates the Latin language of learned publishing in Basel; it does not mean that ordinary conversation throughout the cantons was in Latin.

ending.text: The Old Confederation ended as a political order in 1798. Switzerland continued through new constitutional forms and became a federal state in 1848; the modern country continues. The map’s split between its two labels should not be mistaken for the disappearance and replacement of its people.
